h1: TikTok for Restaurants: A Beginner's Guide to Your First 30 Days
metaTitle: TikTok Marketing for Restaurants: Your First 30 Days
metaDescription: A plain-English, click-by-click guide to TikTok marketing for restaurants: set up your account, know what to film, use trending sounds, and follow a 30-day plan.
heroAlt: A person filming a short food video on a phone in a restaurant
directAnswer: To start TikTok for your restaurant, download the TikTok app, sign up with a business email, then switch to a free Pro account (Profile, the menu icon, Settings and privacy, Account) so you unlock analytics. Fill in your name, bio, city, and a link to your menu. Then post short vertical videos of your food and your staff 3 to 5 times a week, add a trending sound to most of them, and use a few local hashtags like #miamifood. Follow a simple week-by-week plan for the first 30 days so you build a habit instead of burning out.
keyTakeaways: Download TikTok, sign up with a business email, and switch to a free Pro account so you unlock analytics that show which videos actually work.
A Creator account keeps the full trending-song library, while a Business account is limited to TikTok's Commercial Music Library, so pick based on whether trending music matters to you.
Film short, vertical, phone-shot clips: the dish being made, the first bite, your staff, the line out the door. Real beats polished every time.
Post 3 to 5 times a week. Being consistent matters far more than any single perfect video.
Add a trending sound to most videos and a small mix of hashtags, including local ones like #miamifood and #brickelleats plus the name of the dish.
Follow a week-by-week 30-day plan: set up, batch-film, post daily and reply to comments, then double down on whatever got the most views.
intro:
It is a slow Tuesday night. Two of your tables are full, the rest sit empty, and you are leaning on the host stand scrolling your phone. A video of a gooey cheese pull from a spot across town slides by, and it has 400,000 views. You look up at your own dining room, half dark, and think: my food looks better than that. So why is nobody talking about my place?

That gap, between how good your food is and how few people know about it, is exactly what TikTok can close. TikTok is a free app for short vertical videos (the kind you hold your phone upright to watch), and it is very good at putting a video of your food in front of strangers nearby who have never heard your name. You do not need a following, a fancy camera, or a marketing degree. You need a phone and a plan.

This guide is that plan. It walks you through setting up your account click by click, tells you exactly what to film, explains trending sounds and hashtags in plain words, and hands you a simple day-by-day schedule for your first 30 days. By the end of the month you will have a real account, a stack of videos, and a routine you can actually keep.

sections.h2: What can TikTok actually do for a restaurant?
sections.html:
Before you set anything up, it helps to know why this app is worth an hour of your week. TikTok is a free app where people watch short vertical videos, one after another. The screen that matters most is the For You page, which is the main feed TikTok shows every user. Here is the part that is different from almost everything else: TikTok decides what to show people based on what the video is, not on who made it. That means a brand-new restaurant account with zero followers can still land a video in front of thousands of locals.

For a restaurant, that is huge. A tourist standing in Wynwood, a college student in Little Havana, or a couple deciding where to eat in Brickell can all get a video of your birria tacos on their screen without ever having searched for you. People also use TikTok like a search engine now. They type best brunch Miami or where to eat South Beach right into the app and watch what comes back.

So TikTok does two jobs at once. It shows your food to people who have never heard of you, and it answers the question they are already asking, which is simply: where should we eat tonight? In a city as food-obsessed and as camera-happy as Miami, that is a line you want to be standing in.

sections.h2: Should you pick a Business account or a Creator account?
sections.html:
TikTok gives you two free upgraded account types, and both are called a Pro account. A Pro account unlocks analytics, which are simple charts that show how many people saw each video, where they are, and when they are watching. You want analytics, so you want a Pro account either way. The only real decision is which of the two flavors to pick.

  • Creator account. This keeps access to TikTok's full music library, including the mainstream, viral, trending songs everybody is using this week. For most independent restaurants, this is the better choice, because riding trending sounds is one of the biggest reasons a small video suddenly takes off.
  • Business account. This is aimed at brands that advertise. It adds a few tools like scheduling and a website button, but it comes with one big catch: a Business account can only use the Commercial Music Library, which is TikTok's set of tracks pre-cleared for business use. That library does not include most of the chart hits and viral songs. So if you tap a trending sound, a Business account often will not let you post with it.

Our plain advice for a first-timer: start with a Creator account so you can use trending sounds freely. You can always switch later if you begin running paid TikTok ads and want the stricter brand-safe setup. Either way, the setup steps below are almost identical.

sections.h2: How do you set up your restaurant's TikTok, step by step?
sections.html:
Set aside 20 quiet minutes and do this on the phone you will actually film with. Follow the steps in order.

  1. Open your phone's app store, search TikTok, and tap Get or Install. When it finishes, open the app.
  2. Tap Sign up. Choose Use phone or email, tap the Email tab, and enter a business email (not your personal one). Enter your birthday, create a strong password, and type in the 6-digit code TikTok emails you.
  3. Pick a username (this is your handle, the @name). Use your restaurant's real name if you can, like @casalolamiami. Keep it clean and easy to say out loud.
  4. Now upgrade to a Pro account. Tap Profile in the bottom right, then the menu icon (three lines) in the top right, then Settings and privacy.
  5. Tap Account, then tap Switch to Business Account (or look for Creator tools to turn on the Creator account we recommended above). Choose the category that fits, such as Food & Beverage or Restaurant, and finish the short setup.
  6. Go back to your Profile and tap Edit profile. Add a clear profile photo (your logo or a clean shot of your best dish), write a short bio that says what you serve and where you are (for example, Family-run Cuban kitchen in Little Havana), and add your website or menu link in the link field.
  7. Follow a few local restaurants, food creators, and neighbors so your account looks alive, then you are ready to post.

That is the whole setup. If a menu label looks slightly different on your phone, do not worry: TikTok moves buttons around often, but Profile, then the menu icon, then Settings and privacy, then Account is the path that always gets you to the account switch.

This is where most owners freeze. The good news: the videos that work for restaurants are simple, and you already have everything you need to shoot them today. The golden rule is that real beats polished. A slightly shaky phone clip of a real moment will almost always beat a stiff, over-produced ad. Hold your phone vertically, film in good light (near a window or your kitchen line), and keep clips short.

Here are ideas you can shoot this week:

  • The making of one dish. Film the sizzle, the sauce going on, the cheese pull, the final plate. Food in motion stops the scroll.
  • The first bite. A close-up of a fork cutting in, steam rising, a crunch. Sound matters here, so get close.
  • Your people. A bartender making your signature cocktail, the chef plating, a server's honest reaction to a new special. Faces build trust.
  • Behind the scenes. Prep at 8 a.m., the market run, how the empanadas get folded. People love seeing how the food happens.
  • A day or moment in the life. The line out the door on a Friday, a busy brunch, a birthday singalong (with the guests' okay).
  • A quick answer. Point the camera at yourself and answer a real question you get all the time, like what should I order the first time?

You do not need to think all of this up alone. We keep a running list of formats that pull people in, and you can borrow every one of them from our post on restaurant reel ideas that get customers. Same ideas, they work on both TikTok and Instagram.

sections.h2: How do trending sounds work, and what is the rule that trips businesses up?
sections.html:
A trending sound is a song clip or audio bite that a lot of people are using right now. TikTok gives extra reach to videos that use a sound while it is hot, so adding one is one of the easiest ways to get more views. You do not need to be musical, you just need to notice what is trending and tap it on.

Here is how to find and use one:

  1. As you scroll your For You page, watch for the same song showing up again and again. That is a trend forming.
  2. When you see a sound you like, tap the spinning record icon in the bottom right corner of that video. If the sound is climbing, you will often see a small arrow pointing up next to it.
  3. Tap Add to Favorites so you can find it later, or tap Use this sound to start a video with it.
  4. When you record or upload your own video, tap Add sound at the top of the editing screen and pick your trending sound. Lower its volume if you are also talking.

Now the rule that trips people up. As we covered above, a Business account can only use the Commercial Music Library, so many trending chart songs will be blocked or greyed out for you. If you set up a Creator account, you will not hit this wall. If you did choose Business and a sound will not attach, that is why, and it is not a bug. Pick another sound that is available to you, or switch your account type.

sections.h2: How do hashtags work for a restaurant?
sections.html:
A hashtag is a word or phrase with a # in front of it, like #miamifood. It is a label that helps TikTok understand what your video is about and helps people who search that topic find you. You add them in the caption when you post. You do not need a dozen. A small, smart mix beats a wall of random tags.

Use three kinds together, about four to six total:

  • What it is. Describe the food or moment, like #tacos, #brunch, #pastrywindow, or #happyhour.
  • Local. This is your secret weapon as a restaurant, because it points TikTok at the people who can actually walk in. Use tags like #miamifood, #miamieats, #brickelleats, #wynwood, or your neighborhood name.
  • Discovery. One or two broad food tags that lots of hungry people follow, like #foodtiktok or #eeeeeats.

So a video of your birria tacos might read: The birria that people drive across Miami for. #birria #tacos #miamifood #brickelleats #foodtiktok. Keep the caption short and human, and let the hashtags do the sorting.

sections.h2: How often should you post, and when?
sections.html:
Here is the honest answer most people do not want to hear: consistency beats perfection. One amazing video a month will not build anything. A steady drip of decent videos will. Aim for 3 to 5 posts a week when you are starting out. That is roughly one every other day, which is very doable if you film in batches (more on that in the plan below).

A few simple timing tips:

  • Post when your customers are on their phones. For restaurants, that often means late morning as people plan lunch, and early evening (around 5 to 8 p.m.) as they decide on dinner. Weekends are strong for brunch and nightlife spots.
  • Let your own analytics settle it. After two weeks, open your Pro account analytics and look at when your followers are active. Post around those times. Nobody else's schedule matters as much as your own numbers.
  • Do not delete a slow video. TikTok sometimes pushes a clip days or even weeks later. Give every post time to breathe.

If keeping this pace already sounds like one more job you do not have hours for, you are not wrong, and you do not have to do it alone. Handling filming, posting, and replies for restaurants is exactly what our social media management team does, so the account stays alive even on your busiest weeks.

sections.h2: What does a simple 30-day TikTok plan look like?
sections.html:
You do not need to figure out each day as it comes. Here is a four-week plan built for a busy owner. Follow it loosely and you will end the month with a real account and a real habit.

Week 1: Set up and stock up.

  1. Complete the account setup from the steps above (about 20 minutes).
  2. In one slow hour, batch-film 8 to 10 short clips: a dish being made, a first bite, a staff moment, a behind-the-scenes shot. Just capture raw footage, do not worry about editing yet.
  3. Post your first two videos with a trending sound and a few local hashtags.

Week 2: Build the habit.

  1. Post 3 to 5 times this week from the clips you already filmed.
  2. Reply to every comment, even just a heart or a thank you. Comments tell TikTok your video is worth showing to more people.
  3. Film one fresh batch of clips so you never run empty.

Week 3: Read the room.

  1. Open your analytics. See which video got the most views and, more importantly, which held people longest.
  2. Make two or three more videos in that winning style. If the cheese pull worked, film more sizzle and pulls.
  3. Try one talking to camera video answering a common question, so guests hear your voice.

Week 4: Double down and plan ahead.

  1. Keep posting 3 to 5 times a week and leaning into what is working.
  2. Pin your best video to the top of your profile so new visitors see your strongest first (tap the video, tap the three dots, then Pin).
  3. Batch-film next month's clips in one session and jot down five ideas so you are never staring at a blank screen.

Thirty days in, you will not be a viral sensation overnight, and that is fine. You will have something better: a living account, a library of clips, and a rhythm you can keep. That is the foundation every restaurant that wins on TikTok started from.

faqs.q: Is TikTok worth it for a small restaurant?
faqs.a: Yes, for most restaurants TikTok is worth it, because it is free and it shows your food to nearby strangers who have never heard of you. Unlike most platforms, TikTok pushes videos based on the content itself, so a brand-new account with no followers can still reach thousands of local people. People also search TikTok directly for things like best brunch near me. The main cost is your time, so it is worth it as long as you can commit to posting a few short videos a week.

faqs.q: Do I need a Business account or a Creator account for my restaurant on TikTok?
faqs.a: For most independent restaurants, a Creator account is the better pick, because it keeps access to TikTok's full music library, including trending songs that help videos take off. A Business account is aimed at brands that advertise, and it limits you to the Commercial Music Library, which blocks many popular tracks. Both are free and both unlock analytics. Start with a Creator account, and only switch to Business if you begin running paid TikTok ads.

faqs.q: How often should a restaurant post on TikTok?
faqs.a: Aim for 3 to 5 posts a week when you are starting out, which is about one video every other day. Consistency matters far more than any single perfect video, so a steady stream of decent clips will grow your account faster than one polished video a month. Filming in batches (shooting 8 to 10 clips in one hour) makes this pace realistic even on a busy schedule. After two weeks, check your analytics to see when your own followers are active and post around those times.

faqs.q: What should a restaurant film for TikTok?
faqs.a: Film short, vertical clips of real moments: a dish being made, the first bite with steam and crunch, your staff in action, and behind-the-scenes prep. Food in motion, like a sizzle, a sauce pour, or a cheese pull, stops people from scrolling. You can also answer common guest questions on camera, such as what to order first. Real, phone-shot footage almost always beats an over-produced ad, so do not wait for a fancy camera to start.

faqs.q: Do I need special equipment or an editor to make restaurant TikToks?
faqs.a: No. You only need a smartphone and decent light, like a window or your kitchen line. TikTok has all the editing tools you need built into the app, including trimming, captions, and adding sounds. Hold your phone vertically, keep clips short, and film in one take when you can. The videos that perform best usually look real and a little raw, not slick, so simple phone footage is an advantage, not a limitation.

faqs.q: Why can't I use popular songs on my restaurant's TikTok?
faqs.a: If popular or trending songs are greyed out when you try to add them, your account is almost certainly a Business account, which can only use TikTok's Commercial Music Library. That library leaves out most chart hits and viral sounds. It is not a bug or a setting you can override. To use trending songs freely, switch to a Creator account under Settings and privacy, then Account. Restaurants that want to ride trends usually prefer the Creator account for exactly this reason.

faqs.q: How long until TikTok brings in real customers?
faqs.a: Most restaurants should think in terms of months, not days. The first few weeks are about setting up, learning what your audience likes, and building a habit of posting. It is normal for early videos to get modest views. Once you find a style that works and post consistently, reach and foot traffic tend to build over 30 to 90 days. TikTok also sometimes pushes an older video weeks after you post it, so give every clip time and keep going.
